# 16-pairio — sources

Back-test entry `16-pairio.yaml`: Pairio, a voice assistant that helps factory technicians fix broken machines (YC
Spring 2026, P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named
(the launch-era site is in German; its quotes are given in German, with the author's English in brackets). "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-04-21 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one
exists; anything later is marked as later).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Pairio – Fix broken equipment in factories faster", 2026-04-21 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Q18-pairio-fix-broken-equipment-in-factories-faster

- [FAQ] pairio.com FAQ, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com/faq/
- [REF] pairio.com customer reference (Knipping), read 2026-10-22; figures "supplied by Knipping" — https://pairio.com/customer-references/
- [SITE] pairio.com, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Maintenance technicians and operators who fix machines on the production line.
   [LYC] "Pairio helps technicians and operators resolve faults faster with voice AI." [YCP] "AI mobile app that helps
   factory technicians fix broken machines". → `roles[technician]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: the
   technician only (operators are named too, but the fix and the report are the technician's).

2. **What (the job).** Get the machine running again fast, and keep the fix for the next person.
   [LYC] "Unplanned equipment downtime costs global industries over $1.4 trillion every year – and the root cause isn't
   broken machines. It's broken knowledge transfer." [LYC] "With the average technician in the US now 50 years old,
   knowledge is literally walking out the door". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the machine, when it fails, and afterwards when the fix should be written down.
   [LYC] "When a machine fails, resolution speed depends almost entirely on whether the one guy who's seen this before is
   working that day"; "Valuable technical clues are buried somewhere across 400 pages of OEM manuals or locked in outdated
   software"; "After spending 6 hours getting the line back up, the last thing a technician does is sit down and write a
   detailed fault report to institutionalize their knowledge". [FAQ] "Fundamentals and practical ways to use Pairio in
   day-to-day maintenance work." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: machine breakdown`. Author's choice: the window
   {5, WORKING_DAYS} (a working-day rhythm) and Frequency 2 to 4 working days out of 5 -- daily for the team, not for
   each technician (header); Prevalence `p_80_100`.

4. **Which people.** Technicians at US plants that keep their own maintenance team.
   [LYC] "Ask: Can you introduce us to plant and maintenance managers at US manufacturing firms?" [WB] "Pairio richtet sich
   an Unternehmen mit eigener Instandhaltung - vom Mittelstand bis zum Konzern." [Pairio is for companies with their own
   maintenance, from mid-sized firms to groups.] → `context.segment`, `market: US`; the German plants are in the header.

5. **Who pays.** The plant; the maintenance manager chooses, the plant manager agrees.
   [LYC] "If you know anyone in plant operations or maintenance in US manufacturing we'd love to talk with them". [WB]
   quotes a "Meister & Abteilungsleiter Instandhaltung" [foreman and head of maintenance] as a user. → `persona.
   decision_maker: {role: manager}`; Buyer and payer tests "The plant manager" (listed with "The IT department"):
   author's choice, no source names who signs. Purchase friction's tested item, "Connecting it to SAP or Maximo": [FAQ]
   "including systems such as SAP, IFS, IBM Maximo, Oracle EAM Cloud, Hexagon, SharePoint, Outlook, and Asset API"; [WB]
   "Die genaue Anbindung hängt von Ihrer IT-Landschaft ab." [The exact connection depends on your IT landscape.] The IT
   security review and the plant-wide rollout sign-off are the author's. Commitment's step, "run a pilot on one
   production line": [REF] "A clearly scoped pilot creates evidence"; "Following a two-month pilot, the solution was
   integrated in four weeks." (later than launch; the launch-era site offers "Kostenlose Demo" [free demo]).

6. **Mechanism.** Ask by voice or photo; answers from the manuals and past repairs; speak the fix, get a report.
   [LYC] "Simply ask and instantly receive any available technical clue"; "Speak and let Pairio structure their learnings
   into reusable know-how"; "Use photos and videos to capture even more contextual knowledge". [WB] "Sprache, Foto oder
   Video rein - fertiger Bericht raus" [voice, photo or video in, finished report out]; "Pairio erkennt Fehlerbild,
   Maßnahmen, Ersatzteile und erstellt einen strukturierten Bericht." [Pairio recognises the fault, the actions, the spare
   parts and writes a structured report.] [YCP] "Users just take a picture of the broken machine and we search thousands
   of pages of manuals to find the right solution." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (a phone
   allowed at the machine — tested; manuals as files; quiet enough to speak) and Adoption friction (speak the fix when
   done — tested; photograph the fault first) are the author's, from the mechanism's own needs and [BLOG] ("tools that fit
   how technicians actually work, on mobile, in loud environments"). Relative advantage: shorter_time from [WB] "-25%
   MTTR", less_help_needed from [LYC]'s "the one guy who's seen this before"; the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price public; the cost is technician time.
   [WB] "Kostenlose Demo" and "Demo buchen" [free demo; book a demo], no price; [SITE] "Book a free demo", no price.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $600 to $1,200 per technician a year is **the operator's reading** (about $50 to
   $100 a seat a month; header). Existing sacrifice, HOURS 150 to 300 of the breakdowns per technician a year: author's
   arithmetic -- 3 to 6 hours a week of a technician's time lost to hunting through manuals, waiting for the one person
   who knows, extra trips for tools and parts, and the report written afterwards, over about 50 working weeks; the scale
   is set by [LYC]'s "6 hours getting the line back up" and by [WB]'s "-25% MTTR" and "-80% Ablageaufwand" (the shares
   the company says it removes). The rate, $31 an hour, is [BLS] "$30.82 per hour" (May 2025 median), the author's
   stand-in. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [BLOG] "At a specialty manufacturer in Illinois, the maintenance team told me some shifts run with a single
   technician."; "The troubleshooting descriptions? Consistently useless. 'Reset machine.' 'Machine broken, fixed it.'
   'Called supplier.'"; "The work order says there's a problem with the injection molding machine. That's it. They show
   up, assess, go back for parts, come back again."; "When a conveyor goes down, every minute counts in a way that's
   directly visible to the customer."; "she'd watched a technician try to use ChatGPT out of desperation to solve a
   machine-specific problem."

## Status today

Same idea. [SITE] (English, 2026-10-22) describes the same assistant (fault reports, manual search, data analysis, work
instructions) now aimed at US plants, with the Knipping reference: [REF] "Knipping reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) by
25%, generated €500K in savings through avoided downtime, and achieved a 95% adoption rate." and "Four German locations
are already onboarded." [FAQ] "In suitable use cases, MTTR can be reduced by up to 25%, filing effort by up to 80%, and
onboarding time by up to 90%." Price today: still not public ("Book a free demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price.** Nothing public at launch or today; the founder's price is the operator's reading (header, item 7), so the
  Price line measures that reading, not the company's price.
- **A per-plant money cost.** Only the global $1.4 trillion is public; the chain cost is the technicians' time instead
  (header).
- **The hours per technician a year.** The sources give one example (6 hours on one breakdown) and shares removed; the
  150 to 300 is the author's arithmetic.
- **A technician's hour.** [BLS]'s median stands in.
- **Who signs, and the purchase steps.** No source names the buyer above the maintenance manager; the plant manager, the
  IT department, the security review and the rollout sign-off are the author's (the SAP or Maximo connection is sourced).
- **How often one technician meets a breakdown.** "Day-to-day" is the team's rhythm; the 2 to 4 working days out of 5 is
  the author's.
- **First-person technician accounts.** No Launch HN or forum thread; the occasions are scripted from [BLOG] (the
  founder's own account of US visits) and [WB]'s two user quotes ("Mit der App kann ich alles direkt dokumentieren und
  muss mir keine Sorgen machen, dass ich etwas vergesse." [With the app I can document everything straight away and
  needn't worry about forgetting something.]).

founder.order_why: It moves sensibly from where I sell, to the technician's situation, the breakdown problem, my voice-and-photo solution and then who gets asked, so each step builds on the one before.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), split only by the recency screen, so the context felt asked twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asked who pays or how the purchase works: the technician uses Pairio, but the plant pays, the maintenance manager chooses and the plant manager agrees. screens.why1: Right after how it fits the way technicians work, I expect to be asked what it does better, because that is why a plant would switch.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain on first reading, and I can answer at once in my own words: line back up sooner, no waiting for the one guy who knows.
screens.why3: This is my own pitch: I know from my plants and the -25% MTTR what we improve and what technicians do today.
screens.why4: A free box suits this question, 25 words is enough for my two benefits, and 'Leave this out of the study' is a fitting escape.
screens.why5: My answer names two benefits, but the belief Keel shows keeps only 'the line back up sooner' and drops 'fixed without waiting for the expert', which is half of what I sell.
screens.instead: Keep the question and the box, but have the belief carry both benefits: 'For most, their last machine down would have gone better with it: the line back up sooner, fixed without waiting for the expert.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, it's obvious why Keel shows me its draft of those benefits to check before strangers see them.
screens.why2: The rows are shop-floor plain, but "the benefits strangers who say 'better' will tick from" takes a second read, and "All are equal" sits oddly beside a test box that names only the first row.
screens.why3: I hear from technicians and maintenance managers about getting lines back up and waiting on the one person who knows, so I can judge these benefits straight away.
screens.why4: Both rows are distinct and in my trade's words, but the benefit of a finished report without the paperwork, half of what I sell, is missing unless I add it.
screens.why5: Faster repair and not depending on the one guy are my claims kept faithfully, but the list and test drift towards speed alone by dropping the record of the fix.
screens.instead: What it does better than today's way: The line back up sooner / Fixed without waiting for the expert / Fault report done without the paperwork

screens.why1: After fit and advantage, it's the obvious last solution question to ask what a technician must actually do to start using the app, since a tool that adds work after a six-hour repair won't get used.
screens.why2: "What will they have to do to start using it?" is plain on first reading, and the hint's "setup, extra steps or learning" makes clear what counts.
screens.why3: I've watched technicians at our German plants and on my US plant visits, so I know from experience what the app asks of them at the machine and after the fix.
screens.why4: The answer is a free-text box, and "Leave this out of the study" is the right single escape for a founder who doesn't want to test this.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my words "speak the fix into the phone when done", but it silently drops "photograph the fault and ask the app first", and the screen doesn't say that only one step will be tested.
screens.instead: Same question and hint, but show the belief as: "We'll test one step: most would speak the fix into the phone when done. Your other step, photographing the fault first, won't be asked."

screens.why1: Right after I said what technicians must do to start, Keel shows me the steps it drew from that so I can correct them and pick the one to test, which is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: Speak the fix, photograph the fault and install it on the phone are how I describe the product myself, and the instruction to reword, remove or add is clear on first reading, even though the intro repeats the title.
screens.why3: I designed this workflow and have watched technicians at plants, so I know what they would have to do and which step is most likely to fail: speaking the fix once the machine is back up.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and cover the main steps, but 'Photograph the fault and ask the app first' joins two actions, and my technicians can also ask by voice without a photo.
screens.why5: The rows and the belief keep my mechanism and the habit I need to test, that technicians will speak the fix when done, while 'Install it' is only a harmless, plausible addition.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: Install it on their phone; Ask the app by voice or photo when a machine fails; Speak the fix into the phone when done.

screens.why1: Right after I listed what technicians must do to start using it, it makes sense to pick the one effort most likely to stop them, since strangers only get one question on it.
screens.why2: Speak the fix, photograph the fault and install it on the phone are how I talk about the product, and I understand the question on first reading, though "nothing is reworded here" is slightly odd Keel talk.
screens.why3: I've been on plant floors and know that after a long repair, getting a technician to record the fix is the real hurdle, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The list holds my real answer and the efforts are distinct, but "Photograph the fault and ask the app first" bundles two actions into one option.
screens.why5: "Most would speak the fix into the phone when done" is exactly my tested belief, and the bar tests it without changing what I meant.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? Speak the fix into the phone when done / Photograph the fault first / Install it on their phone

screens.why1: At the last step before the study goes out, it is obvious why I am asked whether to end with a request for people to try it, since finding plants to pilot with is exactly what I need.
screens.why2: Pilot is my everyday word, and the hint says exactly what respondents will see and where I will see who said yes.
screens.why3: Whether I want a pilot is entirely my own decision, and a clearly scoped pilot is how I sell.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the complete choice here, the two options are distinct and plain, and no escape chip is needed for a decision that is only mine.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed, but in my business a pilot runs on a production line and the plant manager agrees to it, so a technician leaving an email to 'try this for real' is a softer thing than the word suggests.

screens.why1: Right before people see the study, it makes sense to choose who will ask the questions, and nothing earlier already settled this.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs in video, voice, typing, recording, credits and text links, and it says 'voice' while the choice also fixes the face on video, so I need a second read.
screens.why3: As the founder I can listen to two 5-second samples and judge which interviewer my technicians would stay on with.
screens.why4: Two samples with a preselected default is enough and the options are distinct, but two names tell me nothing about how they differ, such as whether either sounds right for a US plant floor.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'maintenance technicians' and the text-link route exactly as I'd expect, and changes nothing of what I typed.
screens.instead: Who should ask maintenance technicians your questions on video? Daphne (picked for you) or Saskia: hear each for 5 s. Recording the one you pick costs 400 credits either way; people can read and tap instead of talking.

screens.why1: I've just chosen who asks the questions and I'm about to send, so it's obvious why Keel now asks how my technicians should answer.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain on first reading, but "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and "Ready when Daphne is" took me a second read to see that the video is still being made and the voice option can't go out yet.
screens.why3: I've walked these plants and know technicians work on loud floors with a phone in hand, so I can judge between talking and read-and-tap, and the loud-room figure speaks directly to that.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap and letting them choose cover the real choices, are clearly distinct, and need no escape chip because the founder can simply pick one.
screens.why5: It keeps my words "maintenance technicians", changes nothing about my study and says nothing wrong about my product.
screens.instead: How should maintenance technicians answer? AI interviewer Daphne (asks aloud on video; they talk, type or tap; catches more than 9 in 10 spoken answers where it is loud; her video will be ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (they read each question and tap, and can speak or type in any box; ready now) / Let them choose (they pick when they open the link; can be sent once Daphne's video is ready)

screens.why1: I have just chosen how technicians will answer, so the next obvious step is deciding who receives the link.
screens.why2: The question and options are plain on first reading to a founder sending out interviews, and each option explains itself, including the Contacts page I haven't opened yet.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach, namely the technicians and plant contacts I've met on my visits, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and my named-people answer is there, but my likeliest route to more technicians, a maintenance manager passing the link to their team, only loosely fits an open link posted 'where the people already are'.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is kept as typed, with nothing changed about my idea or the technician role.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (each gets their own link) / People I found with Keel (pick a list from a search on the Contacts page; Keel makes a link for each, and you send them) / A group, with one open link (post it where they already are, or give it to a maintenance manager to pass to the team; each person signs in with Google, then is interviewed)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with its deciding number beside it (4 answered, 5 needed on each card), so I know no belief has been called and why.
screens.why_b2: The stage page draws no chart, but the tally and cards show what is counted and the bar of 5; '7 people answered' against '4 answered' takes a second look because nothing says why three are missing.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction each carry the exact belief line I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: it never says to get at least one more counted answer on each belief, or that my solution is neither confirmed nor refuted.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the answers, keeps n visible and says plainly the counts are too low to call, though it leaves the 3 uncounted people unexplained.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of your 7 were counted on each belief and 5 are needed, so send the study to more technicians who had a machine down this week before you trust or change the solution.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted with 5 needed, and the So line repeats it, so I know there is no answer yet and why.
screens.why_b2: The four options, the 4 counted and the zero against read at once, but "your bar · 3 of 4" beside a rule of "no more than 1 in 3" takes a second look, because the same bar is given as a count of yes answers and as a share of no answers.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "a phone was allowed at the machine" are exactly what I checked on the way in, and the question uses my trade's own words, "last machine down".
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is honest and "5 needed" hints at one more counted answer, but it never tells me to get that answer, or to make sure it includes plants that restrict phones on the floor.
screens.why_b5: Four yeses out of four are not called a win, the small n is stated ("a lean, not a call"), and Travis's excluded guess is shown openly.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted said a phone was allowed, but 5 are needed, so get one more clear answer, ideally from a plant that restricts phones on the floor, before relying on this.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is plain and "4 counted, 5 needed" decides it, but the line under the verdict says "4 answered" while the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", so I have to stop and work out that five people did answer and Travis's guess is why it falls short.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 against Same 1 over 4 people reads at once, but the bar needs a second look: "3 of 4" is where I landed, while the rule is written the other way round as "no more than 1 in 3" against, so I have to do the sum to see I'd clear it.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the line about the last machine down and the line back up sooner are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is true but generic: it never says one more counted answer would settle it, or what to do about Bogdan's point that planned work and short staffing eat his week.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond the people who answered: n stays visible, the guess is left out and named, the small group is called a lean rather than a call, and the answer is flagged as a hypothetical asked with Pairio in mind.
screens.instead: Under the verdict say "5 answered, 4 counted, 5 needed: Travis's answer was a guess", then: "3 of 4 say it would have gone better, which is over your bar if it holds, so get one more technician's answer about a real breakdown, and ask whether planned work and short staffing matter more, as Bogdan says."

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' and the So line repeats it as 4 counted, 5 needed, though '4 answered' above jars with '5 answered · 4 counted' below.
screens.why_b2: The answers and the 4 counted are plain, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads like both the result and the bar, and the ghost cell takes a second look to tie to Travis.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Adoption friction and carries my line word for word: most would speak the fix into the phone when done.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' implies I need one more counted answer but does not say so, or tell me what to do about the end-of-shift objection.
screens.why_b5: n and the small group are stated and nothing is called held, but the 3 of 4 looks like it clears the bar while Travis, the one person left out, says plainly he would not do it, and counting him would make it 2 of 5 against, over the 1 in 3 limit, which the screen does not say.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted would speak the fix, but Travis (not counted, his story was a guess) says that after a hot, loud shift he just wants to clock out, and counting him would put you over the 1 in 3 limit, so get a few more technicians with a clear last breakdown and ask whether they would speak the fix at the end of a shift.

screens.why_b1: Each box states "Too few to call" with "4 answered · 5 needed to call it" right beside it, so the non-verdict and the number deciding it are both plain.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and Adoption friction are the names I saw, and both belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "5 needed to call it" implies I need one more answer, but nothing says what these two objections mean for the idea, such as whether to rethink the moment the report is captured.
screens.why_b5: Nothing claims beyond the four people, and Travis is honestly marked as not counted, but Adoption friction's "1 against" sits above a lone quote tagged "not counted", so at first read I can't tell whether anyone counted is against.
screens.why_b6: With only two quotes, they still add what I did not type: my most senior technician says planned work and short staffing eat the week, and speaking the fix fails at clock-out, not just because of the noise.
screens.instead: Under Adoption friction, say "1 counted against, but no quote from them; the only reason here is from someone not counted", and end each box with "One more answer settles this; meanwhile, these are single voices: ask whether senior technicians gain anything and whether the fix can be captured before the end of the shift."

screens.why1: A first question checking whether my plant keeps its own maintenance crew makes sense, since a study about maintenance work would want to know that up front.
screens.why2: Plant and maintenance team are the words I use every day, and I get it on the first read, though someone at a plant that also uses a few contractors might pause for a second.
screens.why3: I know without thinking whether our plant has its own maintenance guys because I'm one of them.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it for a screening question, the two don't overlap, and no escape is needed because anyone working at a plant knows the answer.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of plants running their own maintenance teams and tells me nothing about any product or who is behind the study.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and I can answer yes or no after hearing it once, though saying 'I'll read 2 options' for a yes-or-no is a little stiff.

screens.why1: After asking if my plant runs its own maintenance, it makes sense to ask if I've had a machine go down lately before asking me to tell the story.
screens.why2: I get it right away, but "did you have" is a little loose because a line machine going down is usually the plant's, not mine, so I'd wonder if it means one I worked on or any on the line.
screens.why3: Machines going down is my everyday work, so I can answer for the last week from memory.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chip "I can't recall one particular machine down" reads awkwardly, and "I'd rather not say" is a second escape on a simple gate that should not need any.
screens.why5: It stays on a machine going down on the line in the last 5 working days, and nothing about any product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, ends in "Yes or no," and I'd answer it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a machine on your line go down that you worked on? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I had a machine go down, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it, and the card says plainly it is a new part.
screens.why2: I know manuals, wiring diagrams, fault reports, SAP and Maximo, but "an answer and fault report" is a clumsy name for a thing and "answers with the source" takes me a second read.
screens.why3: Digging through manuals and past repairs at the machine and then writing up the fix is my actual day, so I can picture this against what I do.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options to choose from.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea card and says what it does and what its builders believe, with nothing slipped in where it should not be.
screens.why6: It can be said and followed, but it runs long for one hearing, with the list of symptoms, actions and spare parts and then SAP, Maximo or SharePoint, and the last sentence repeats what I just heard.
screens.instead: Imagine Pairio, an assistant on your phone for machine fixes. You ask by voice or photo, and it searches manuals, wiring diagrams and past repairs and tells you where the answer came from. You talk through the fix or take photos, and it writes the fault report into SAP, Maximo or SharePoint. The people building it believe this would get you answers at the machine and a proper record of the fix.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, it makes sense to ask whether a phone was even allowed at the machine, since a phone rule would decide whether I could use this on the floor.
screens.why2: "Last machine down" and "phone at the machine" are plain to me, but "allowed ... easily" reads a little crooked, and the card's "answer and fault report" doesn't tell me much.
screens.why3: I know the phone rules on my floor and whether I had mine on me on the last breakdown, so I can answer from that.
screens.why4: "Yes, with some steps" is vague for a phone rule and runs close to "Only with help or approval", though the true answer is there and "I can't tell" fits.
screens.why5: "Pairio, an answer and fault report" is a shown idea so no leak, but it says little of what the thing is and the phone question assumes a phone app I was never plainly told about.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and four short options I can hold after one hearing, with the escape said last.
screens.instead: Think of your last machine down. Were you allowed to use your phone at the machine? Yes; yes, with a supervisor's okay; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the phone question, it makes sense to ask whether this thing would have helped on the breakdown I just had.
screens.why2: I get the question, but "machine down" as a noun is a little clipped, and "go better" is vague: faster fix, or an easier write-up?
screens.why3: I know how my last breakdown went, but with only "an answer and fault report" to go on, I'd be partly guessing at what Pairio would have done for it.
screens.why4: The four options are distinct and cover the range in plain words, and "I can't tell" fits since I've never used it.
screens.why5: It reads as the founder's idea on purpose and nothing leaks, but "go better" drifts from getting the machine running fast and leaving a record of the fix.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, with four options I can hold after one hearing and a clear escape at the end.
screens.instead: Would Pairio have got your last machine down back up sooner, or not? A lot sooner; a little sooner; no difference; or it would have slowed me down. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking if I could have my phone at the machine and if this would have helped, asking whether I'd actually do the one thing it needs from me is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Speaking the fix into my phone when I'm done is plain shop talk and I get it the first time I read or hear it.
screens.why3: I close out jobs and write up fixes all the time, so I know whether I'd talk one into a phone with the line back up and the next call waiting.
screens.why4: The choices cover it and I can't tell fits, but Yes, if it was clearly worth it sits oddly among the plain answers and overlaps with Probably not, since that's how I'd hedge either way.
screens.why5: It is the idea card's product doing what the card said, asked as a step I would take, with no founder's plan or talk about people like me coming through.
screens.why6: It's two short sentences and one question, with four short options I can hold in my head and one escape said last.
